In our [CNN article](../../ml/deep-learning/cnn-from-pixels-to-yolo.qmd) we saw how YOLO draws boxes around objects in a single pass. The field has moved quickly since then. In 2026 a detector can run on a phone, reach record accuracy on a server, find objects you describe in plain words, and fuse cameras with lidar in a moving car. This article maps the landscape and shows which tool fits which job, from reading a barcode to driving through fog.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The five detection tasks and how they differ
- The four model families that define the state of the art in 2026
- How to read accuracy (mAP), speed (latency) and the trade-off between them
- How to pick a confidence threshold for your use case
- Eight real use cases, from barcode reading to driverless cars, with recommended approaches
:::

## The four families of 2026

| Family | Leading models | Big idea | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Real-time CNN detectors** | YOLO26, YOLO12 | Small, fast, easy to export to phones and edge chips | Cameras, robots, embedded devices |
| **Real-time transformers (DETR family)** | RF-DETR, D-FINE, DEIM, RT-DETR | Attention instead of hand-made anchors; no NMS step | Highest accuracy at real-time speed on a GPU |
| **Open-vocabulary and promptable** | Grounding DINO, YOLOE, SAM 3 | Find objects described by text or an example image | Changing products, rare objects, fast labelling |
| **Vision foundation backbones** | DINOv3 | One huge self-supervised model whose features power many tasks | Specialised domains with few labels |

: The state-of-the-art detection landscape in 2026 {#tbl-families}

A few milestones behind that table:

- **YOLO26** (January 2026) predicts boxes end-to-end without non-maximum suppression by default, and one family covers detection, segmentation, classification, pose, depth and oriented boxes ([Ultralytics](https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/)).
- **RF-DETR** from Roboflow, built on DINOv2 features and deformable attention, is described as the first real-time model to exceed 60 AP on the COCO benchmark ([Roboflow on GitHub](http://github.com/roboflow/rf-detr)).
- **D-FINE-L** reaches 54.0 AP at 124 frames per second on an NVIDIA T4 GPU ([Roboflow Playground](https://playground.roboflow.com/models/ustc/d-fine)), and **DEIMv2-S** is the first model under 10 million parameters to pass 50 AP ([DEIMv2 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.20787)).
- **Grounding DINO** detects objects from text and scores 52.5 AP on COCO without ever training on COCO ([IDEA Research](https://github.com/IDEA-Research/GroundingDINO)).
- **SAM 3** from Meta finds, segments and tracks every instance of a concept given as a short phrase or example image; SAM 3.1 (March 2026) tracks up to 16 objects in one pass ([Meta AI](https://ai.meta.com/blog/segment-anything-model-3/)).
- **DINOv3** (August 2025) was trained without labels on 1.7 billion images, with a 7-billion-parameter flagship and small distilled versions ([Meta AI](https://ai.meta.com/blog/dinov3-self-supervised-vision-model/)).

## Reading the scoreboard: accuracy vs speed

Detectors are compared on **COCO** (80 everyday object types) using **mAP@50:95**: average precision, averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. Higher means boxes are both correct and tight. Speed is **latency**, the milliseconds to process one image; frames per second is $1000 / \text{latency}$.

$$
\text{mAP}_{50:95} = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{t \in \{0.50, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\}} \text{AP}_{\text{IoU} \ge t}
$$ {#eq-map}

Set the frame rate your application needs. Models that are too slow fade out.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
board = pd.DataFrame([
    ("YOLO26-N", "CNN", 1.7, 40.1, 2.4), ("YOLO26-X", "CNN", 11.8, 56.9, 55.7),
    ("YOLO12-N", "CNN", 1.6, 40.4, 2.5), ("YOLO12-L", "CNN", 5.83, 53.8, 26.5),
    ("RF-DETR-N", "Transformer", 2.3, 48.4, 30.5), ("RF-DETR-M", "Transformer", 4.4, 54.7, 33.7),
    ("RF-DETR-2XL", "Transformer", 17.2, 60.1, 126.9),
    ("D-FINE-L", "Transformer", round(1000 / 124, 1), 54.0, None), ("D-FINE-X", "Transformer", round(1000 / 78, 1), 55.8, None)],
    columns=["model", "family", "latency_ms", "map", "params_m"])
ojs_define(board=board.drop(columns="params_m").to_dict(orient="records"))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof fps = Inputs.range([10, 400], {value: 60, step: 5, label: "Required frames per second"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
budget = 1000 / fps
fit = board.filter(d => d.latency_ms <= budget)
best = d3.greatest(fit, d => d.map)
Plot.plot({

  x: {type: "log", label: "Latency per image on NVIDIA T4 (ms, log scale) →", domain: [1.2, 25]},
  y: {label: "↑ COCO mAP 50:95", domain: [38, 62]},
  color: {domain: ["CNN", "Transformer"], range: [ms.teal, ms.indigo], legend: true},

    Plot.rectX([{x1: budget, x2: 25}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 38, y2: 62, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.06}),
    Plot.ruleX([budget], {stroke: ms.rose, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
    Plot.text([budget], {x: d => d, y: 39, text: () => `${budget.toFixed(1)} ms budget`, dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: ms.rose, fontSize: 12}),
    Plot.dot(board, {x: "latency_ms", y: "map", fill: "family", r: 7, fillOpacity: d => d.latency_ms <= budget ? 0.95 : 0.18}),
    Plot.text(board, {x: "latency_ms", y: "map", y: d => d.map + ({"YOLO12-N": 0.7, "YOLO26-N": -0.7, "YOLO12-L": -0.8, "D-FINE-L": 0.7, "YOLO26-X": 0.6, "D-FINE-X": -0.6}[d.model] ?? 0), text: "model", dx: 9,
      textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11.5, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: d => d.latency_ms <= budget ? 1 : 0.3})
  ]

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>At ${fps} fps the most accurate option is</span><b>${best ? best.model : "none"}</b><span>${best ? best.map + " mAP" : "lower the frame rate"}</span></div>`
```

Figures come from the [JetBrains 2026 comparison](https://blog.jetbrains.com/pycharm/2026/07/best-object-detection-models-for-machine-learning-in-2026/) and, for D-FINE, the [Roboflow Playground](https://playground.roboflow.com/models/ustc/d-fine). Measurement setups differ slightly, so treat close values as ties and **always re-test on your own images**.

## Choosing a confidence threshold

Every detection comes with a confidence score. Where you set the cut-off decides the trade-off between **precision** (of the boxes we report, how many are real?) and **recall** (of the real objects, how many did we find?). The right point depends on the cost of each mistake.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n_true = 400
scores_tp = np.clip(rng.beta(6, 2, n_true), 0, 1)        # detections that match a real object
found = rng.random(n_true) < 0.93                         # 7% of objects never get a box at all
scores_fp = np.clip(rng.beta(2, 5, 500), 0, 1)           # false alarms (background, reflections)
ojs_define(det=dict(tp=np.round(scores_tp[found], 3).tolist(), fp=np.round(scores_fp, 3).tolist(), n_true=n_true))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof thr = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "Confidence threshold"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pr = d3.range(0.02, 0.99, 0.01).map(t => {
  const tp = det.tp.filter(s => s >= t).length, fp = det.fp.filter(s => s >= t).length;
  return {t, precision: tp / Math.max(1, tp + fp), recall: tp / det.n_true};
})
cur = {
  const tp = det.tp.filter(s => s >= thr).length, fp = det.fp.filter(s => s >= thr).length;
  const p = tp / Math.max(1, tp + fp), r = tp / det.n_true;
  return {tp, fp, fn: det.n_true - tp, p, r, f1: 2 * p * r / Math.max(1e-9, p + r)};
}
html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>Precision</span><b>${(cur.p * 100).toFixed(0)}%</b><span>Recall</span><b>${(cur.r * 100).toFixed(0)}%</b><span>False alarms</span><b>${cur.fp}</b><span>Missed objects</span><b>${cur.fn}</b></div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  ...msStyle, height: 320,
  x: {label: "Recall →", domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%"}, y: {label: "↑ Precision", domain: [0.4, 1.01], tickFormat: "%"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(pr, {x: "recall", y: "precision", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.dot([cur], {x: "r", y: "p", r: 9, fill: ms.amber, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.text([cur], {x: "r", y: "p", text: () => `threshold ${thr.toFixed(2)}`, dy: -16, fill: "currentColor", fontSize: 12})
  ]
})
```

A **pharmacy pill counter** cannot miss a pill, so it uses a low threshold and accepts a human check of false alarms. A **retail checkout** that charges a customer wants high precision. A **self-driving car** wants both, which is why it adds more sensors instead of trusting one threshold.

### Niche case: reading barcodes

Barcodes look trivial, but warehouse cameras see dozens per frame, at angles, under plastic wrap. The modern recipe splits the job: a **detector** finds where codes are, and a **decoder** reads the bars. OpenCV's barcode module can load a super-resolution network to sharpen small crops before decoding ([OpenCV docs](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d6/d25/tutorial_barcode_detect_and_decode.html)).

```{.python filename="read_barcodes.py"}
import cv2, zxingcpp

img = cv2.imread("parcel.jpg")
# find and decode every code in the image
for code in zxingcpp.read_barcodes(img):
    print(code.format, code.text, code.position)
```

For very hard images, train a small YOLO model to find codes first, crop each box, and pass the crops to the decoder.

### Critical case: driverless cars

A self-driving car must detect objects in **3D**, know how fast they move, and never be blinded by one failure. Waymo's 6th-generation Driver uses **13 cameras, 4 lidars and 6 radars** ([Waymo](https://waymo.com/blog/2024/08/meet-the-6th-generation-waymo-driver/)). Its foundation model uses a "Think Fast, Think Slow" design: a sensor-fusion encoder fuses camera, lidar and radar over time for fast reactions, while a driving vision-language model trained with Gemini reasons about rare scenes such as a burning vehicle ahead ([Waymo](https://waymo.com/blog/2025/12/demonstrably-safe-ai-for-autonomous-driving/)). Tesla takes a different path: cameras only, with one end-to-end network from pixels to steering ([vFuture Media](https://vfuturemedia.com/electric-vehicles/tesla-vision-only-self-driving-2026-inside-ai-powered-fsd-strategy/)).

Why combine sensors? Try this toy bird's-eye-view simulator. Each sensor has a different range and weakness. Add fog or night and watch which objects are still seen.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sensors = Inputs.checkbox(["Camera", "Lidar", "Radar"], {value: ["Camera", "Lidar", "Radar"], label: "Sensors"})
viewof fog = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Fog density"})
viewof night = Inputs.toggle({label: "Night", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
road = [
  {id: "car ahead", x: 60, y: 0, kind: "vehicle"}, {id: "truck", x: 150, y: -8, kind: "vehicle"},
  {id: "cyclist", x: 35, y: 10, kind: "small"}, {id: "pedestrian", x: 22, y: -16, kind: "small"},
  {id: "car behind", x: -45, y: 4, kind: "vehicle"}, {id: "deer", x: 105, y: 22, kind: "small"},
  {id: "fast car", x: 235, y: -4, kind: "vehicle"}, {id: "child", x: -10, y: 14, kind: "small"}
]
range = ({
  cam: 160 * (1 - 0.8 * fog) * (night ? 0.45 : 1),
  lidar: 200 * (1 - 0.6 * fog),
  radar: 250
})
FOV = 0.6   // front camera half-angle in radians
seenBy = o => {
  const d = Math.hypot(o.x, o.y), out = [];
  const front = o.x > 0 && Math.abs(Math.atan2(o.y, o.x)) < FOV && d < range.cam;
  if (sensors.includes("Camera") && (front || d < range.cam * 0.3)) out.push("C");     // long-range front + short surround
  if (sensors.includes("Lidar") && d < range.lidar) out.push("L");
  if (sensors.includes("Radar") && d < (o.kind === "vehicle" ? range.radar : 70)) out.push("R");
  return out;
}
view = road.map(o => ({...o, s: seenBy(o)}))
circle = r => d3.range(0, 361, 3).map(a => ({x: r * Math.cos(a * Math.PI / 180), y: r * Math.sin(a * Math.PI / 180)}))
Plot.plot({
  ...msStyle, height: 330, width: 760, marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 20, clip: true,
  x: {domain: [-70, 260], label: "metres ahead →"}, y: {domain: [-50, 50], label: "↑ metres left"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect([{}], {x1: -70, x2: 260, y1: -7, y2: 7, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.06}),
    sensors.includes("Lidar") ? Plot.line(circle(range.lidar), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: ms.teal, strokeDasharray: "4,4", strokeOpacity: 0.7}) : null,
    sensors.includes("Camera") ? Plot.line([{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: range.cam * Math.cos(FOV), y: range.cam * Math.sin(FOV)}, {x: range.cam, y: 0}, {x: range.cam * Math.cos(FOV), y: -range.cam * Math.sin(FOV)}, {x: 0, y: 0}], {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeOpacity: 0.7, strokeDasharray: "2,3"}) : null,
    sensors.includes("Camera") ? Plot.line(circle(range.cam * 0.3), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: ms.indigo, strokeOpacity: 0.4, strokeDasharray: "2,3"}) : null,
    Plot.dot([{x: 0, y: 0}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 9, symbol: "square", fill: ms.amber}),
    Plot.dot(view, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 7, fill: d => d.s.length >= 2 ? ms.teal : d.s.length === 1 ? ms.amber : ms.rose, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.text(view, {x: "x", y: "y", text: d => `${d.id} ${d.s.length ? "(" + d.s.join("+") + ")" : "(missed)"}`, dy: -13, fontSize: 11, fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>Seen by 2+ sensors</span><b>${view.filter(d => d.s.length >= 2).length}</b><span>by only 1</span><b>${view.filter(d => d.s.length === 1).length}</b><span>missed</span><b style="color:${ms.rose}">${view.filter(d => d.s.length === 0).length}</b><span>of ${view.length}</span></div>`
```

The orange square is our car. Dashed lines show each sensor's reach: the front camera's long cone plus short surround cameras (C), lidar's 360° circle (L), and radar (R), which sees vehicles far away but small objects only up close. Teal objects are confirmed by two or more sensors, amber by one, red are missed. Turn off lidar and radar, then add fog: a camera-only car loses distant objects first. This is a simplified toy, not a model of any real vehicle, but it shows why redundancy matters when lives are at stake.

## Getting started in code

::: {.panel-tabset}
## YOLO26 (edge, fast)
```{.python filename="yolo26_detect.py"}
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")                     # nano model, runs on CPU
results = model("dock.jpg")                    # boxes, classes, confidences
model.train(data="my_data.yaml", epochs=50)    # fine-tune on your images
model.export(format="onnx")                    # deploy anywhere
```
## RF-DETR (top accuracy)
```{.python filename="rfdetr_detect.py"}
from PIL import Image
from rfdetr import RFDETRBase

model = RFDETRBase()                            # COCO-pretrained
detections = model.predict(Image.open("dock.jpg"), threshold=0.5)
print(detections.class_id, detections.confidence)
```
## YOLOE (open vocabulary)
```{.python filename="yoloe_prompt.py"}
from ultralytics import YOLOE

model = YOLOE("yoloe-26s-seg.pt")
model.set_classes(["package with barcode", "safety cone"])   # any words
results = model.predict("dock.jpg")
```
:::

Code patterns follow the [Ultralytics YOLO26 docs](https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/), the [RF-DETR repository](http://github.com/roboflow/rf-detr) and the [YOLOE docs](https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yoloe). Check licences before commercial use: Ultralytics models are AGPL-3.0 unless you buy an enterprise licence, while RF-DETR's base sizes are Apache 2.0.

## How to choose

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TD
  A["What must the model find?"] --> B{"Fixed list of objects?"}
  B -- "No, it changes" --> C["Open vocabulary:<br/>YOLOE, Grounding DINO, SAM 3"]
  B -- Yes --> D{"Where does it run?"}
  D -- "Phone, drone, edge chip" --> E["YOLO26 N/S<br/>export to TFLite, CoreML, TensorRT"]
  D -- "Server GPU" --> F["RF-DETR or D-FINE<br/>for top accuracy"]
  E --> G["Fine-tune on your own images"]
  F --> G
  C --> H["Use it to auto-label,<br/>then train a small fast model"]
  H --> G
```

A popular 2026 workflow combines the families: use a large promptable model such as SAM 3 or Grounding DINO to **auto-label** thousands of images, check them by hand, then train a small, fast YOLO or RF-DETR model to run in production.

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | Fix |
|---|---|
| Trusting COCO scores for your domain | Benchmark on a sample of your own images |
| One global confidence threshold | Tune per class and per cost of error |
| Ignoring licences | Check AGPL, Apache and custom licences before shipping |
| Small objects in huge images | Tile the image or raise input resolution |
| Testing only in good conditions | Collect night, rain, glare and motion-blur samples |

## Summary

- Detection covers **boxes, masks, oriented boxes and open-vocabulary prompts**, not just labels.
- **YOLO26** leads on edge speed, **RF-DETR** and the DETR family lead on real-time accuracy, **SAM 3** and **YOLOE** find what you describe, and **DINOv3** supplies general-purpose features.
- Compare models with **mAP** (@eq-map) and latency, then choose a **confidence threshold** that matches the cost of mistakes.
- Use cases range from a **barcode decoder** on a phone to **multi-sensor 3D perception** in a driverless car; the stakes decide how much redundancy you need.
